# Modeling and inferring human trust in automation based on realtime eye tracking data

Yidu Lu and Nadine Sarter University of Michigan, Ann Arbor

Trust miscalibration remains a major challenge for human-machine interaction. It can lead to misuse or disuse of automated systems. To date, most trust research has relied on subjective ratings and behavioral or physiological data to assess trust. Those trust measurements are discrete, disruptive and quite difficult to implement. To better understand the process of trust calibration, we propose eye tracking as an unobtrusive method for inferring trust levels in real time. Using an Unmanned Aerial Vehicle simulation, participants were exposed to varying levels of reliability of an automated target detection system. Eye movement data were captured and labeled as high or low trust based on subjective trust ratings. Feature extraction and raw eye movement data were compared as input for multiple classification modeling methods. Accuracy rates of 92% and 80%, respectively, were achieved with individual-level and group-level modeling, suggesting that eye tracking is a promising technique for tracing trust levels.

## INTRODUCTION

Trust miscalibration remains a major challenge for human-machine interaction. It can lead to misuse or disuse of automated systems (Parasuraman & Riley, 1997). Trust has been defined as “the attitude that an agent will help achieve an individual’s goals in a situation characterized by uncertainty and vulnerability” (Lee & See, 2004). To better understand trust in human-automation interaction, a variety of measurement techniques have been employed. The majority of past studies have relied on subjective ratings to infer participants’ trust levels (Merritt & Ilgen, 2008). Subjective ratings have the advantage of being easy to implement. However, they are quite disruptive and therefore not well suited for real-world applications. Other studies recorded behavior, such as reverting to manual control, as indicators of trust in automated vehicle studies (Brown & Noy, 2004). The main limitation of this approach is that behavioral measures are specific to a task or domain and thus do not generalize and cannot be compared across experiments. More recently, attempts have been made to infer trust in real time based on various psychophysiological measures. Research has shown that measures such as electroencephalography (EEG) and galvanic skin response (GSR) can be used to build models of human trust in modern technologies (Ajenaghughrure, Sousa, Kosunen, & Lamas, 2019; Hu, Akash, Jain, & Reid, 2016). In both studies, once participants’ trust reached a stable level, the model achieved a mean accuracy of over 70% in predicting people’s trust level in real time. Still, the process of setting up for collecting some of these data is quite involved, and the equipment is rather intrusive and uncomfortable.

To address the shortcomings and limitations of the above approaches, we propose to use real-time eye tracking data instead or in addition to more traditional techniques. Various eye tracking metrics/features have been widely used as indicators of cognitive processes such as decision making (Vachon & Tremblay, 2014), workload (Marshall, 2002) and situation awareness (Moore & Gugerty, 2010). One of the main benefits of using eye tracking is that it affords real time collection and processing of eye movement data. Another advantage is its non-invasive nature (Rayner, 1998). Compared to other physiological measurements, the setup of an eye tracker is quite easy and unobtrusive.

To date, there is limited empirical evidence for the feasibility and validity of using eye tracking data to infer human trust in automation (Hergeth, Lorenz, Vilimek, & Krems, 2016; Lu & Sarter, 2019). The promising results from these studies were usually based on post-hoc statistical analysis. More research is needed to establish whether modeling techniques such as machine learning can be applied to eye tracking data to infer operators’ trust levels in real time. Real-time assessments are important as they allow for the development of adaptive alert systems that respond to observed trust miscalibration and resulting breakdowns in monitoring.

Eye tracking metrics extracted from raw eye movement data have proved to work well as input to various modeling methods. For example, pupil diameter has been used to predict performance on various information search and integration tasks in real-time, using a random forest method (Buettner, Sauer, Maier, & Eckhardt, 2018). Another study used ten unique features extracted from raw eye movement data as input and compared the performance of seven classifying methods in detecting personality traits, including AdaBoost, Decision Tree, Logistic Regression, Naive Bayes, Random Forest, Support Vector Machine, and k-Nearest Neighbor (Berkovsky et al., 2019). In most of these studies, the datasets used as input for the modeling process were based on groups of participants because the classifying algorithms require large data samples to train the model and achieve relatively high and stable performance. This “generalized” modeling process is appropriate in many cases. However, prediction accuracy with this approach can suffer due to large inter-individual differences in the dataset (Krull & MacKinnon, 2001). Also, very few studies to date have used raw eye movement data as input to machine learning models in order to make predictions. One benefit of modeling raw eye tracking data, rather than processed eye tracking features, is that this approach is more generalizable to a wide range of tasks and settings.

To address the limitations previously mentioned, the current study examined the performance of two different modeling processes: 1) using eye tracking metrics from individuals for “personalized” modeling, and 2) using eye tracking metrics from a group of participants for “generalized” modeling. In the latter case, two types of input data were compared: 1) using defined eye tracking metrics, and 2) using raw eye movement data (gaze point coordinates). The choice of eye tracking metrics used in the present study - fixation duration percentage and transition count - were based on earlier research (Lu & Sarter, 2019). In terms of classification modeling methods, there is no agreement on which methods are preferable. The utility of each method heavily depends on the data to be modeled. In this study, Linear Regression (LR), k-Nearest Neighbor (kNN), Random Forest (RF), Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) were compared to determine which method can achieve the highest accuracy. LR was used as the baseline comparison in each modeling process due to its simplicity. kNN returns classification labels by comparing the feature similarity between the new sample and labeled training data sample using Euclidean distance. It works well with a relatively small number of features. RF classifies a new sample based on the vote result from many trained decision trees. Bagging and feature randomness ensure its modeling performance. These two methods have been used successfully in other application domains using eye tracking data as input. They both require little data preprocessing and parameter handling. The two deep learning approaches, MLP and CNN, were employed in this study for modeling the raw eye tracking data because they are well suited for identifying the intricate structure of large data sets and have been shown to dramatically improve the modeling results in various application domains (LeCun, Bengio, & Hinton, 2015).

Figure 1 provides an overview of the modeling process and classification methods used in this study.

Figure 1. Modeling process overview

In summary, the goal of this research was to answer the following research questions:

Can eye tracking data serve as an indicator of different trust levels?

Is modeling at an individual level more effective than modeling at the group level?

Can using raw eye tracking data as input for the modeling process achieve the same level of performance as using defined eye movement features?

Which modeling algorithm works best for inferring trust levels based on eye tracking data?

## METHOD

## Experiment task

The experiment was conducted using a computer-based Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) control simulation. Participants were asked to complete two tasks at the same time: a visual search task and a tracking task (see Figure 2). For the visual search task, participants were instructed to monitor the video feeds from 8 unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) to detect the appearance of military targets. Participants were told that automation onboard the UAVs would help them with the detection of a target. The border of the video feed would change to red when the UAV identified a possible target. The border would turn green when the automation reached a potential target region but did not detect a target. The target was defined as a black truck carrying a gun (See Figure 3). A black truck without a gun, which looks very similar to the target, was included in the video feeds to function as a distractor and increase the difficulty of the task (See Figure 3).

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Figure 2. Simulation

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Figure 3. Target vs non-target

When a video feed was highlighted, participants had to decide whether or not to review the scene. If they did, they then had to press one of two buttons (Ö or ´) to either agree or disagree with the automation assessment regarding the presence of a target. If the participant decided to trust the automation and not review the scene, the automation would proceed with its own determination. Independent of whether the participant reviewed the scene and responded to the automation suggestion, they would receive auditory feedback regarding the accuracy of the automation assessment.

In parallel with the visual search task, participants had to perform a tracking task (adopted from MATB-II (NASA)) in the center of the screen (see Figure 2). For this task, participants’ goal was to keep the smaller target circle inside the two larger circles around the origin of the coordinate frame using a joystick. They were informed that a UAV might crash if the target circle moved outside the larger circles.

Participants were instructed to treat the visual search task and the tracking task as equally important and to try to achieve the best possible performance on both tasks.

## Data collection

A total of 20 participants from the University of Michigan participated in this experiment. Their average age is 22.2 years (SD=3.55), and 12 of them are males. Participants were required to have normal or corrected-to-normal vision. Contact lenses were acceptable but not eyeglasses due to the use of the eye tracker. The eye tracking data were collected using Tobii Pro Glasses 2 at a sampling rate of 50 Hz. After signing the consent form and being trained on the two tasks, baseline eye tracking data were collected during a high (95%) and a low (50%) automation reliability scenario for modeling purposes. Each scenario lasted for 6 minutes, and participants were informed about system reliability in advance. The sequence in which the two reliability levels were experienced was randomized.

## Data processing and modeling

Three types of data sets were tested as input for the modeling process shown in Figure 1. One data set consisted of eye tracking metrics from each individual participant, the second set combined eye tracking metrics from all participants, and the third set used the raw eye movement data from all participants.

Based on findings from a previous study (Lu & Sarter, 2019), two eye tracking metrics were used as extracted feature: fixation duration percentage and transition count. Fixation duration percentage is the percentage of time that a participant focuses on the area where the visual search task is presented (AOI 1 in Figure 4). Transition count refers to the number of transitions between AOI 1 (Area of Interest 1: the visual search area) and AOI 2 (the tracking task area; see Figure 4).

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Figure 4. AOI definition

For the raw eye movement dataset, each data sample includes only the coordinates of raw gaze points in the form of (x,y). Data were pre-processed, including dealing with missing data, down-sampling and standardization, before they were entered as input. Each missing data point was filled with the previous data point. The whole dataset was down-sampled from 50 Hz to 1 Hz using average pooling, i.e., calculating the average x, y value for every 50 raw eye movement points. Input standardization was performed on these data points.

For all types of model input, a moving time window of one minute was used. Based on extensive piloting, one minute of eye movement data was found to be long enough to reflect participants’ current trust level. Successive time windows were overlapped by ten seconds to implement the trust level modeling in real time.

Incomplete data from 4 of the 20 participants were discarded, leaving 16 data sets for modeling purposes. For individual-level modeling, the data from the first three minutes were used as the training set. Data from the next 90 seconds were used as the validation set to select the most appropriate parameters in the model. The data collected during the last 90 seconds were used as the test set. In group-level modeling, data from 4 out of 16 participants were randomly selected as test sets. For model selection, we applied twelve-fold cross validation which means that, in each model training process, data from eleven groups of participants were used as the training set and the last group was used as the validation set. This process was repeated twelve times so that each group was used once as the validation set. The overall validation performance was the average from the twelve trials.

For the feature extraction data set, three classification methods were employed: Logistic Regression (LR), k-Nearest Neighbors (kNN) and Random Forest (RF). These methods were applied using standard implementations from the Python library “Scikit-learn” (Pedregosa et al., 2011).

Finally, for the raw eye movement data set, LR, MLP and CNN were compared. MLP and CNN were tested in this stage due to their outstanding learning capabilities. They were implemented using TensorFlow (Abadi et al., 2016). Specifically, we used an MLP with two hidden layers. Each hidden layer has 32 units with Relu activations. Batch normalization was applied after each hidden layer. The output layer had two output units and Softmax activation. For CNN, we used one 1-D convolutional layer with 4 kernels of size 7, followed by a fully connected layer with 16 units. Both the convolutional layer and the fully connected layer used Relu activations. As with MLP, batch normalization was applied after each hidden layer. The output layer has two output units and Softmax activation.

## RESULTS

In this section, results for each of the three modeling processes are presented. The performance of each classifying method was assessed by comparing the accuracy of inferring trust levels in the test datasets.

## Individual level modeling using eye tracking metrics

Figure 5 shows the results of three classifiers when using eye tracking metrics as input to model at an individual level. RF achieved the highest average accuracy rate at 92.97% (SD = 0.047). The mean accuracy for 16 participants when using kNN was 92.19% (SD = 0.053). And logistic regression resulted in a mean accuracy rate of 90.63% (SD = 0.059).

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Figure 5. Individual level modeling using eye tracking metrics

Group level modeling using eye tracking metrics

The modeling accuracy of the three classification methods applied at a group level, using eye tracking metrics as input, is shown in Figure 6. RF achieved the highest accuracy rate at 81.51% (SD = 0.077). The accuracy of using kNN was 80.70% $( SD  = 0.130 )$ , and accuracy with logistic regression was the lowest with an accuracy rate of 77.52% (SD = 0.055).

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Figure 6. Group level modeling using eye tracking metrics

Group level modeling using raw eye movement data

The accuracy of the three classification methods when using raw eye movement data as input is shown in Figure 7. CNN outperformed the other methods and achieved an accuracy rate of 80.72% $(  SD  = 0.096 )$ in inferring trust levels. MLP and LR did not perform well when using raw eye movement data as input. The accuracy rate was substantially lower compared to CNN: 60.64% (SD = 0.031) and 44.12% (SD = 0.041), respectively.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Figure 7. Group level modeling using raw eye movement data

## DISCUSSION

Trust miscalibration remains one of the main challenges for appropriate use of, and reliance on modern technologies. To be able to better support trust calibration, an unobtrusive method for inferring trust in real time is needed. In this study, eye tracking was used for this purpose. The findings from this research indicate that 1) eye tracking is indeed a promising method for inferring trust levels in real time, 2) modeling at an individual level outperformed modeling at a group level using two eye tracking metrics as input, and 3) at a group-level, both raw eye movement data and eye tracking metrics work reliably (achieving an accuracy of around 80%) for inferring high or low trust levels, using machine/deep learning techniques.

The three modeling processes used in this research achieved an accuracy of at least 80%, demonstrating the feasibility of using eye tracking data to infer trust in real time. The much higher accuracy achieved with individual level modeling, compared to generalized modeling, suggests the existence of significant individual differences due to dispositional factors affecting operators’ trust in automation (Merritt, Heimbaugh, LaChapell, & Lee, 2013; Merritt & Ilgen, 2008). These individual differences need to be taken into account when forming collaborative human-machine teams.

When using eye tracking metrics as input, the accuracy of LR, kNN and RF did not differ a lot. However, other aspects of these techniques, such as their modeling efficiency, modeling variance and interpretability should also be considered when selecting one method for use in real-world environments. Modeling efficiency matters when real-time inference is required at very short intervals and a large dataset needs to be modeled. The variance in the modeling results reflects the stability of the modeling performance. A high degree of stability is desirable for creating an adaptive alerting system to support trust calibration. And past research has established that transparency and interpretability are important factors affecting the adoption of advanced technologies (Wright, Chen, & Lakhmani, 2019). Thus, when the performance of different classification models is nearly the same, preference should be given to models whose output can be easily interpreted and understood by human operators.

The generalized modeling results indicate that data collected from one group of operators can be applied, to an extent, to other cohorts. Even though not as accurate as personalized modeling, generalized modeling was still rather effective at over 80% accuracy. This means that, in situations where training and collecting individual baseline data is not feasible, trust modeling and inference is still possible to an extent using this method. Also, with more data samples being collected over time and added to the modeling process, the accuracy of this approach may well increase over time.

Based on our findings, it appears that using raw eye movement data as input to the modeling process can result in similar levels of accuracy as using eye tracking metrics. The increasing performance from LR to MLP demonstrates that non-linear transformation of raw data is required for classifying raw eye movement data. The increase in performance from MLP to CNN illustrates that incorporating the inductive bias of temporal invariance can further improve the performance of the classifier. Our eye tracking-based approach outperforms the use of EEG and GSR in an earlier study for building a trust classification model (Akash, Hu, Jain, & Reid, 2018). The fact that the performance of grouplevel modeling was similar when using either extracted features or raw data supports the robustness of deep learning algorithms. It suggests that the complex and time-consuming feature extraction step may not be needed to achieve high performance.

Some limitations of this study need to be highlighted. First, only a limited number of algorithms were explored; future studies should examine the effectiveness of additional modeling techniques to identify the most preferable method(s). Also, the effectiveness of the modeling methods studies in this research need to be tested for other tasks and different application domains to ensure their robustness.

Overall, the findings from this study add to the knowledge base in trust in modern automation technologies. They provide a new tool for conducting research in this area. Importantly, our eye-tracking based method can help infer trust and detect changes in operators’ trust levels in real time. This is critical for developing techniques to help operators calibrate their trust in automation and monitor and collaborate with automation in a more efficient way. In turn, this will lead to more appropriate adoption of modern technologies and benefit society by resulting in safer operations in a variety of application domains.
